title: Time series of tip, width and fluctuation: how does the flame fluctuate?
summary: Three stacked traces sharing one time axis: a height, a width and the height's deviation from its mean, with the sampling rate stated. It shows rhythm, amplitude and whether the signals move together.

media.alt: Three stacked time-series panels sharing a time axis: tip height, flame width and tip fluctuation, each oscillating at about seven hertz, with a stated sampling rate.
media.caption: Reference render with synthetic demonstration data (design-system gallery).

source.note: Plot class from the design system's plot taxonomy; synthetic demonstration data.

read_the_figure.question: How does the flame fluctuate?
read_the_figure.axes: Shared x: time in s (0 to 2). y: tip height in mm, flame width in mm, and tip fluctuation (height minus its mean) in mm, one panel each. Text: sampling rate 500 Hz, N = 1000 samples; dotted amber line is the mean.
look_at: How many cycles in the window, and so what is the dominant frequency?
What is the peak-to-peak amplitude of each trace?
Do the width and the height peak together or in opposition?
What sampling rate and number of samples are quoted?
read_the_figure.proves: The traces show how the flame breathes: frequency, amplitude, phase between quantities. With a stated sampling rate the reader can tell what frequencies could be present at all.
if_wrong: No sampling rate or units: the time axis cannot be related to frequency.
A sampling rate too low (below twice the signal frequency): the signal is aliased.
Different y scales hiding that one signal is much larger: compare amplitudes in the same units.

terms.meaning: Number of samples per second, f_s in Hz.
Highest frequency that can be represented, f_s / 2.
The signal minus its time mean; shows variation about the average.
The frequency at which most of the variance sits, counted from cycles over time or from the spectrum.
Root of the mean of the squared fluctuation; a single number for amplitude.

remember: Window length T = N / f_s = 2 s; frequency resolution 1/T = 0.5 Hz.
Fluctuation = signal - mean; RMS = sqrt(mean of x'^2).

understand.title: Marks and encodings
understand.text: Position along the shared time axis encodes time. Vertical position in each panel encodes the measured quantity; colour and line style (solid, dashed, dash-dot) distinguish the traces. The dotted amber line is the mean of the tip height. The note at the upper left states the sampling rate and the number of points.

understand.title: Why this form answers the question
understand.text: Fluctuation is a pattern in time, and a line against time is the most direct view. Stacking the traces on one axis lets the eye compare timing between them without a cross-correlation. The fluctuation trace is the same as the height trace after the mean is subtracted: it puts the amplitude on a symmetric zero line.

understand.title: Read this reference render
understand.text: Q1: What is the dominant frequency? Counting peaks of the tip height, about 14 cycles occur in the 2 s window, so f_0 = 7 Hz (period 0.143 s). Q2: What are the amplitudes? Tip height runs between about 37 and 46 mm, so about 9 mm peak to peak around a mean of 42 mm; the width runs between 10.5 and 13.5 mm, 3 mm peak to peak. Q3: Are width and tip locked together? The width oscillates at the same 7 Hz as the tip, so the two are locked together; the peaks do not fall at exactly the same instants, the offset being a small fraction of the 0.14 s period (read it from a few neighbouring peaks, or compute a cross-correlation).

understand.title: The must-check list, explained
understand.text: Units and sampling rate: the figure states mm on each axis and f_s = 500 Hz with N = 1000, so the reader can compute the time span, the Nyquist frequency and the resolution. Without them the series is a shape without a scale.

understand.title: How it misleads
understand.text: Different y ranges per panel make a small signal look as large as a large one. Without the sampling rate the reader cannot say what frequency is resolvable. A short window (2 s) gives a poor frequency estimate and misses slow trends. A trace with noise can look like a pattern; line plots hide the distribution of values. Aliasing produces slow wiggles from fast signals.

understand.title: Alternatives
understand.text: A power spectrum of the fluctuation (peak at the dominant frequency), an autocorrelation, or a phase plot of width against height (a loop) shows the phase relation. A histogram of values shows the distribution.

understand.title: A variant to create
understand.text: Add the spectrum in a fourth panel with a log y axis and mark the dominant frequency and the Nyquist limit.

worked.title: Reading frequency and amplitude from the trace
worked.problem: The tip height has 14 cycles in 2 s with components of 3 mm at 7 Hz and 1.2 mm at 23 Hz plus noise of 0.5 mm. What are f_0, the Nyquist frequency and the RMS fluctuation?
worked.answer: 7 Hz, 250 Hz, 2.3 mm. The 23 Hz term appears as the small wiggles on each cycle.

checks.q: N = 1000 samples at 500 Hz. Window length and frequency resolution?
A 480 Hz oscillation is sampled at 500 Hz. What does the trace show?
checks.answer: An apparent 20 Hz oscillation: the signal is aliased because 480 Hz is above the Nyquist limit of 250 Hz.
